glance.label: Main Idea
glance.html: With no Israelite army in the field, the LORD humbles Dagon in his own temple and lays His heavy hand on the Philistine cities until they plead to send the ark of the God of Israel away.

glance.label: Setting
glance.html: The Philistines have just defeated Israel and captured the ark (4:10–11). They carry it to Ashdod, one of their five chief cities, and set it in the house of their god Dagon as a trophy of victory.

glance.label: Chapter Outline
glance.html:
• 1 Samuel 5:1–5 — Dagon Falls Before the Ark

  • 1 Samuel 5:6–12 — The Hand of the LORD Heavy on the Philistine Cities

glance.label: Key Verse
glance.html: “But the hand of the LORD was heavy on the people of Ashdod, and He ravaged them and struck them with tumors, both Ashdod and its territory.” (1 Samuel 5:6, NKJV)

cards.title: The Heart of the Chapter
cards.html:
Chapter 4 ended with the cry that the glory had departed from Israel. Chapter 5 shows that the LORD’s glory had not been defeated. The Philistines set the ark beside Dagon, as though Israel’s God now stood as a captive in their god’s house. The next morning Dagon is found “fallen on its face to the earth before the ark of the LORD” (5:3), and his worshipers have to lift him back into place. The following morning his head and both palms lie broken off on the threshold (5:4). A god who must be propped up by his worshipers cannot stand in the presence of the living God.

Then the scene widens from the idol to the people. “The hand of the LORD was heavy on the people of Ashdod” (5:6), and as the ark moves from Ashdod to Gath and on to Ekron, tumors, panic and death follow it. No priest carries it and no Israelite soldier fights for it. The LORD acts alone. Israel’s sin had brought defeat, but the LORD still defends His own name, and the Philistines learn that His hand is heavier than any power they trust. The chapter closes as “the cry of the city went up to heaven” (5:12).

cards.title: Chapter Sections
cards.html:
1 Samuel 5:1–5 — Dagon Falls Before the Ark

The Philistines carry the ark to Ashdod and set it beside Dagon, but on two mornings the idol lies fallen on its face before the ark of the LORD, the second time with its head and hands broken off. The idol’s severed hands stand in contrast to the powerful hand of the LORD that follows, and the threshold of Dagon’s house becomes a lasting reminder of that morning.

1 Samuel 5:6–12 — The Hand of the LORD Heavy on the Philistine Cities

The LORD strikes the people of Ashdod with tumors, and each city that receives the ark, first Gath and then Ekron, suffers under the same heavy hand. The Philistine lords finally plead for the ark of the God of Israel to be sent back to its own place, while the cry of the stricken city rises to heaven.

cards.title: Why This Chapter Matters
cards.html:
This chapter shows that God’s honor does not depend on the strength of His people. Israel had failed and the ark sat in enemy hands, yet the LORD needed no army to defend His name. That truth humbles us, because God cannot be used, and it comforts us, because our failures do not overthrow Him.

The chapter also exposes idolatry for what it is. Whatever people set beside the LORD will finally fall before Him, whether it is an image of stone or anything else we trust in His place. Isaiah later mocks idols that must be carried by those who worship them (Isaiah 46:1–7), and Dagon lying broken on his own threshold gives that truth a vivid picture.

cards.title: Key Themes to Watch For
cards.html:
The LORD acts alone. God works in Philistine territory without priest, army or Israelite help (5:1–12).

The helpless idol. Dagon falls, is set back in place, and falls again broken (5:3–4).

The heavy hand of the LORD. The image of God’s hand recurs as His judgment spreads from city to city (5:6–7, 9, 11).

Fear without repentance. The Philistines recognize God’s hand against them but seek only to be rid of the ark (5:7–8, 10–11).

cards.title: Key Words & Concepts
cards.html:
Dagon. The chief god worshiped at Ashdod. The popular picture of Dagon as a fish-shaped god and the proposed meanings of his name are uncertain; the chapter’s point is that he cannot stand before the LORD (5:2–4).

Ashdod, Gath and Ekron. Three of the five main Philistine cities, each struck in turn as the ark is moved (5:1, 8, 10).

The threshold. The doorway of Dagon’s house where the idol’s head and hands lay. The priests’ custom of not stepping on it kept the memory of his fall alive (5:4–5).

Tumors. Swellings that broke out on the people of each city (5:6, 9, 12). Together with the golden rats of 6:4–5, they suggest some kind of plague, but the exact disease cannot be identified with certainty. The text’s emphasis is that the LORD struck them.

Lords of the Philistines. The rulers of the Philistine cities, who meet twice to decide what to do with the ark (5:8, 11).

focus: Chapter 5 shows the LORD humbling Dagon and striking the Philistine cities while the ark is in their land, without any Israelite army, until the Philistines plead for the ark to be sent away.

sections.title: Dagon Falls Before the Ark
sections.summary: The Philistines bring the ark from Ebenezer to Ashdod and set it beside Dagon. On two mornings Dagon lies fallen on its face before the ark, the second time with its head and hands broken off.

items.title: What the Morning Revealed
items.html: Twice the narrator takes us straight to the morning: “when the people of Ashdod arose early in the morning, there was Dagon, fallen on its face” (5:3; also 5:4). We are not shown the moment Dagon fell, and no human action is described. The decisive work is reported only by its results. That is worth noticing. God’s purposes can advance without public activity, visible excitement or anyone watching. This is not a rule that God always works quietly, and not every quiet season hides a miracle. But the absence of something we can see never proves the absence of God’s work. Some of what He is doing in my life I will only see “in the morning,” when the results are already there. Spurgeon pictured the temple quiet after the day’s celebration, with Dagon falling in the stillness of the night. The text does not describe that scene; it reports only what was found in the morning. But Spurgeon used the picture to urge his hearers to give the word they had heard time to work in quiet thought, because much of what God does in us happens when we stop and consider what He has said. “Be still, and know that I am God” (Psalm 46:10).
items.q: Twice the narrator takes us straight to the morning: “when the people of Ashdod arose early in the morning, there was Dagon, fallen on its face” (5:3; also 5:4).

items.title: Religious Activity Is Not Divine Life
items.html: In this section the Philistine worshipers are busy. They carry sacred objects, arrange the temple, restore the image and keep their customs. Dagon does nothing. The LORD acts decisively. The contrast is more than one religion against another. It is the difference between human religious activity and the activity of the living God. Religious practices can be meaningful expressions of faith, but they cannot produce divine life. Jesus told people who studied the Scriptures carefully, “you are not willing to come to Me that you may have life” (John 5:40). The goal of religious practice is a living relationship with God.
items.q: In this section the Philistine worshipers are busy.

items.title: The God Who Carries Us
items.html: Dagon’s priests had to lift their god back into place. Isaiah draws the contrast sharply. The idols of Babylon are loaded onto weary animals, but the LORD says to His people, “Even to your old age, I am He, and even to gray hairs I will carry you! I have made, and I will bear” (Isaiah 46:4). False religion puts the burden of keeping the god alive on the worshiper. True faith rests on the God who sustains the worshiper. The Christian life is not held together by our ability to keep God close through perfect performance. It rests on His faithfulness, grace and sustaining power. We obey, but obedience is never an attempt to keep God strong or faithful. We serve because He first carries us.
items.q: Dagon’s priests had to lift their god back into place.

items.title: Patience Is Not Weakness
items.html: The humiliation of Dagon unfolded over two mornings, not all at once. God’s power does not always appear as immediate and total destruction. He reveals, exposes and acts according to His own timing. The fact that God has not yet brought a matter to its end does not mean He lacks the power to do it. “The Lord is not slack concerning His promise, as some count slackness, but is longsuffering toward us” (2 Peter 3:9).
items.q: The humiliation of Dagon unfolded over two mornings, not all at once.

items.title: When Christ Comes In, the Idols Must Fall
items.html: Spurgeon preached this section in a sermon called “Dagon’s Ups and Downs.” He saw the ark entering Dagon’s temple as a picture of Christ entering a person’s soul: when the living God is present, the old ruling idols cannot keep their place. Scripture shows the pattern again and again. In Ephesus, new believers brought their books of magic and burned them in public (Acts 19:19). The Holy Spirit reveals the glory of Christ, and as Christ becomes better known and more treasured, competing trusts are exposed. But this does not happen automatically, and it is more than a feeling in a worship service. The Ephesians confessed and burned their books. Paul calls believers to “put to death the deeds of the body” by the Spirit (Romans 8:13), and John ends his first letter, “Little children, keep yourselves from idols” (1 John 5:21). God’s presence exposes the idol; repentance, obedience and the Spirit’s power put it away. That is why time in His presence can become uncomfortable. It is meant to be. Spurgeon also noticed that the ark came into the temple while Dagon still sat on his throne. Grace does not wait for us to clear out our idols first. Paul says God “made us alive together with Christ” “even when we were dead in trespasses” (Ephesians 2:5). The Lord comes in while sin still reigns, and then the idol begins to fall.
items.q: Spurgeon preached this section in a sermon called “Dagon’s Ups and Downs.”

items.title: God’s Glory Shines Through Human Failure
items.html: Israel had dishonored God through disobedience and presumption. The Philistines had dishonored Him through false worship. Neither failure kept God from revealing His glory. Human failure can be grievous and costly without being the final word over God’s purposes. God remains faithful to Himself. His purposes do not rest on our perfection, even though our obedience matters deeply.
items.q: Israel had dishonored God through disobedience and presumption.

sections.title: The Hand of the LORD Heavy on the Philistine Cities
sections.summary: The hand of the LORD is heavy on Ashdod, striking its people with tumors, and the ark is sent on to Gath and then Ekron, bringing deadly destruction wherever it goes. The Philistines gather their lords and plead for the ark of the God of Israel to be sent back to its own place.

groups.title: The Hand of the LORD Heavy on the Philistine Cities

items.title: The Hand Moves City by City
items.html: “The hand of the LORD” or “the hand of God” appears four times in this section (vv. 6, 7, 9, 11). It grows from “heavy” to “very heavy” as the ark moves from Ashdod to Gath to Ekron. Every city that receives the ark wants to be rid of it. God’s dealings came in stages, as the plagues once moved through Egypt. The text does not say so directly, but God’s character suggests that each stage was also an opportunity to turn to Him. God’s judgments or discipline can come in stages, and each stage is a call to turn to Him. Have I missed an earlier call, and is He calling again?
items.q: Have I missed an earlier call, and is He calling again?

items.title: Holiness Without a Mediator
items.html: The Philistines had priests of their own (5:5), and in the next chapter they consult priests and diviners about what offering to send (6:2–3). What they lacked was the way God Himself had given for sinners to approach Him. In Israel the ark stood in the Most Holy Place, beneath the mercy seat where the high priest sprinkled the blood of atonement on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16:14–15). In Philistia the ark stood among people who had none of God’s appointed provision for dealing with sin. This contrast is a spiritual reading drawn from the rest of Scripture, not something chapter 5 states. But it fits the larger story: without the covering God provides, His holy presence is a weight no one can bear. Paul says God set Christ forth “as a propitiation by His blood, through faith” (Romans 3:25). A propitiation is a sacrifice that turns away God’s just anger against sin. Christ’s blood fully dealt with our guilt, so that sinners can come to the holy God in peace instead of fear. The Philistines knew God’s hand as heavy to judge; in Christ, we know it as mighty to save.
items.q: The Philistines had priests of their own (5:5), and in the next chapter they consult priests and diviners about what offering to send (6:2–3).

items.title: Corporate Crisis Should Lead to Corporate Humility
items.html: The affliction struck whole communities, but their response centered on managing the ark. Scripture shows another way. When Jonah warned Nineveh, the whole city, from the king down, humbled itself and turned from evil (Jonah 3:5–10). In chapter 7, Israel will gather at Mizpah, confess, “We have sinned against the LORD,” and seek Him through Samuel’s prayer (7:6). The Philistines responded together, but not with humility. When trouble comes on a church, a family or a nation, our first response should be to humble ourselves before God together.
items.q: The affliction struck whole communities, but their response centered on managing the ark.

items.title: From Confidence to Fear, but Not to Repentance
items.html: At the start of the chapter the Philistines held the ark as a trophy. In Ashdod they recognized that God’s hand was against them and their god (5:7). The lords learned from Gath that moving the ark did not help (5:9–11). By the time it reached Ekron, its arrival caused immediate terror (5:10). The ark had not changed, and the LORD had not changed. What changed was the Philistines’ understanding of what the ark represented. They had plenty of evidence. Their problem was not ignorance but resistance; their responses were still governed by loyalty to Dagon and a desire for relief. The chapter records recognition, fear and a decision to send the ark away. It does not record any city turning to the LORD. Recognizing God is not repenting. “Even the demons believe—and tremble!” (James 2:19). A person can collect testimonies and spiritual experiences and still resist God in the same area of life. What matters is not only what God reveals, but how we respond to it. Is there an area where I have recognized God’s hand without yet turning to Him?
items.q: Is there an area where I have recognized God’s hand without yet turning to Him?

items.title: When Fear Becomes a Community’s Identity
items.html: The people of Ekron reacted as one. The ark had become a symbol of danger throughout the region, and the city’s shared perception shaped its reaction before anything else happened. Communities form shared ideas about God. Some are shaped by faith, thanksgiving and trust. Others are dominated by fear, suspicion or misunderstanding. Spiritual leaders play an important role in helping people form a biblical understanding of God’s character, so that experience alone does not define Him.
items.q: The people of Ekron reacted as one.

items.title: A Victory Without a Conversion
items.html: The chapter could have ended with the Philistines abandoning Dagon and confessing the LORD as God. Instead it ends with suffering and a decision to send the ark away. The LORD has been vindicated, but the chapter records no one turning to Him. Divine victory and human salvation are not the same thing. God may display His glory through judgment, but judgment is not redemption. The gospel shows that God is glorified not only in righteous judgment but also in the salvation of those who turn to Him through Christ. Scripture’s story of Ashdod does not end with chapter 5. Centuries later, after Philip had baptized the Ethiopian official, “Philip was found at Azotus,” the Greek name for Ashdod, “And passing through, he preached in all the cities till he came to Caesarea” (Acts 8:40). The city where Dagon lay broken became a place where the good news of Christ was preached. Acts does not tell us how many there believed, and 1 Samuel does not predict Philip’s visit. But the contrast is worth holding. In chapter 5 Ashdod saw its idol exposed and still sent God away; in Acts it heard the message of reconciliation. Our calling is not only to show that people’s idols cannot save. It is to announce the One who can.
items.q: The chapter could have ended with the Philistines abandoning Dagon and confessing the LORD as God.

whole.title: The Captive Who Conquered
whole.html: At the end of chapter 4, everything seems to say that Israel’s God has lost. In chapter 5, God shows that His enemies’ apparent victory was never a victory over Him. The temple meant to proclaim Dagon’s triumph becomes a courtroom where Dagon’s claims are judged and exposed. There are seasons when circumstances seem to contradict everything we know about God. The danger is to interpret God’s character from the circumstances instead of interpreting the circumstances in light of God’s character. A temporary appearance of defeat does not tell us what God is finally doing. That is supremely true of the cross. Jesus was rejected, condemned and crucified, and it looked like the end. Yet through His death and resurrection He defeated sin and death. The ark was a sacred object, and Jesus is the Son of God who willingly gave Himself for sinners. Still, the pattern is the same: what looks like God’s defeat can be the very shape of His victory.
whole.q: At the end of chapter 4, everything seems to say that Israel’s God has lost.

whole.title: God Defends His Own Honor
whole.html: In chapter 4 Israel tried to use the ark to win a battle and lost. In chapter 5 no Israelite army marches, no Israelite priest intervenes on God’s behalf, and no prophet speaks. The only priests in the chapter are Dagon’s (5:5). Israel’s own priesthood had just been judged: Hophni and Phinehas were dead, and Eli died at the news (4:11, 18). The narrator then reports Dagon’s fall without recording any human hand at work, and nobody preaches to the Philistines. Matthew Henry observed that Israel made no recorded effort to recover the ark; God acted to vindicate His own honor. God ordinarily works through His people, and their obedience matters. But their failure did not weaken Him, and their absence did not leave Him helpless. “Not by might nor by power, but by My Spirit,” says the LORD of hosts (Zechariah 4:6). David would later tell Goliath, “the battle is the LORD’s” (1 Samuel 17:47). This frees us. We are called to proclaim God’s truth faithfully, but we do not hold up His glory. A pastor who carries the church as if it would collapse without him, or a believer who feels he must win every argument to protect God’s name, can put that burden down. God is quite able to defend His own honor. Spurgeon pointed out that God’s jealousy has two sides. It brought discipline on Israel in chapter 4. But when the Philistines claimed that Dagon had beaten the LORD, the same jealousy turned against His enemies. When God’s name is mocked, His people can take comfort that He will not let His honor be trampled forever.
whole.q: In chapter 4 Israel tried to use the ark to win a battle and lost.

whole.title: The Presence We Cannot Control
whole.html: Israel tried to use the ark as a charm (4:3). Philistia tried to add it to its temple, then manage it, then ship it away. Both made the same mistake. God cannot be used, collected or managed. He will be treated as holy, or He will show Himself holy. To some His presence is “the aroma of life leading to life,” and to others “the aroma of death leading to death” (2 Corinthians 2:16). When Israel failed to guard the ark, God guarded it Himself. A person can be deeply religious and still try to control the terms of his relationship with God. What is the difference between inviting God into my plans and surrendering my plans to His rule?
whole.q: What is the difference between inviting God into my plans and surrendering my plans to His rule?

whole.title: Psalm 78 and the Larger Story
whole.html: Psalm 78 retells this period of Israel’s history. It recounts Israel’s unfaithfulness and says God “forsook the tabernacle of Shiloh” and “delivered His strength into captivity, and His glory into the enemy’s hand” (Psalm 78:60–61). Then “the Lord awoke as from sleep, like a mighty man… and He beat back His enemies” (78:65–66). God was not helpless when the ark was captured. He allowed it as His judgment on Israel. His later action in Philistia was not an attempt to win back power He had lost; it revealed power He had always had. The psalm then moves to God’s choice of David, the shepherd-king (78:70–72). The larger story runs from failed leadership and judgment to God’s provision of a shepherd for His people, and ultimately to Jesus, the Son of David and the Good Shepherd.
whole.q: Psalm 78 retells this period of Israel’s history.

whole.title: The Weight of God’s Glory
whole.html: In Hebrew, the word for “glory” (kabod) comes from a root meaning weight or heaviness. The same root runs through these chapters. God says, “those who honor Me I will honor” (2:30). Israel mourns, “The glory has departed from Israel” (4:22). In chapter 5 the LORD’s hand is “heavy” on Philistia (5:6, 11). In chapter 6 the Philistine priests advise, “give glory to the God of Israel” (6:5). Israel failed to honor God, and the Philistines tried to honor Dagon, yet God made the weight of His own glory impossible to ignore. Human beings do not create God’s glory by worshiping Him. Our worship acknowledges it, and our disobedience dishonors Him, but neither changes who He is. The question is not whether God is glorious. The question is whether our lives respond rightly to His glory.
whole.q: In Hebrew, the word for “glory” (kabod) comes from a root meaning weight or heaviness.

whole.title: One Standard of Holiness
whole.html: It would be a mistake to think the Philistines suffered because they were Gentiles, while Israel could enjoy God’s presence automatically. Chapter 4 has already shown Israel under severe judgment. In chapter 6, when men of Beth Shemesh looked into the ark, the LORD struck them, and they asked, “Who is able to stand before this holy LORD God?” (6:19–20). Later Uzzah died when he reached out to steady the ark (2 Samuel 6:6–7). God does not have one standard of holiness for Israel and another for Philistia. Covenant privilege brings real blessing, but it never gives God’s people permission to treat Him lightly. “Be holy, for I am holy” (1 Peter 1:16).
whole.q: It would be a mistake to think the Philistines suffered because they were Gentiles, while Israel could enjoy God’s presence automatically.

whole.title: Conviction That Leads to Transformation
whole.html: The Philistines felt God’s presence as pure discomfort and wanted the ark removed. The believer’s response to the Holy Spirit should be different. When the Spirit convicts, He does not merely make sin uncomfortable. He reveals Christ and leads us into a new way of life. Jesus said of the Spirit, “He will glorify Me” (John 16:14). As we behold the Lord’s glory, we “are being transformed into the same image from glory to glory, just as by the Spirit of the Lord” (2 Corinthians 3:18). It is not enough to have an idol exposed. We need the Spirit to renew our minds, change our desires and produce the fruit of Christlike character (Galatians 5:22–23). Conviction is not meant to become an endless cycle of guilt and avoidance. It is meant to lead to repentance, renewed fellowship and obedience. Can God’s work be recognized in me without being obeyed?
whole.q: Can God’s work be recognized in me without being obeyed?

whole.title: Discernment Asks What an Experience Means
whole.html: The Philistines experienced overwhelming displays of divine power. They knew something supernatural was happening. Yet they did not respond with faith and obedience. That is a valuable warning for those who value spiritual experiences and manifestations. The reality or intensity of an experience does not by itself show that the heart has responded rightly to God. Spiritual discernment must be able to tell what is really going on, not just describe the facts. It weighs the truth revealed, its agreement with Scripture, the character of God and the response it produces. “Do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits, whether they are of God” (1 John 4:1). The goal of spiritual experience is deeper knowledge of God, greater love for Christ and obedience to His Word.
whole.q: The Philistines experienced overwhelming displays of divine power.

whole.title: God Cannot Be Confined to Our Buildings
whole.html: The Philistines treated sacred space as if it could settle the ranking of the gods. But the LORD could not be confined by Dagon’s building. Solomon later prayed, “heaven and the heaven of heavens cannot contain You. How much less this temple which I have built!” (1 Kings 8:27). Paul told the Athenians that God “does not dwell in temples made with hands” (Acts 17:24). The church must keep the same distinction. Buildings and sanctuaries are valuable for their purpose, but God’s presence is not controlled by architecture. Jesus said true worshipers “will worship the Father in spirit and truth” (John 4:23).
whole.q: The Philistines treated sacred space as if it could settle the ranking of the gods.

whole.title: Use Him or Escape Him
whole.html: Chapters 4 and 5 show two opposite errors. In 4:3 Israel brought the ark into battle, hoping its presence would guarantee victory. In 5:7 the Philistines wanted it gone because its presence had become unbearable. Israel wanted the benefit of God’s presence without the faithfulness He required. Philistia wanted distance from His presence because it refused to yield to Him. Both treated the location of the ark as the central issue. One tried to use God; the other tried to escape Him. The biblical alternative is to know Him, honor Him, trust Him and obey Him. Which error am I more prone to?
whole.q: Which error am I more prone to?

whole.title: Wanting God Himself
whole.html: The Philistines wanted their suffering to stop and the ark to leave. The narrative never shows them seeking to know the LORD. That raises one of the deepest questions in the life of faith: do I want God for what He can do for me, or for who He is? There is nothing wrong with bringing our needs to God; Scripture invites us to do it again and again. But David shows where faith is meant to grow: “One thing I have desired of the LORD… that I may dwell in the house of the LORD all the days of my life, to behold the beauty of the LORD” (Psalm 27:4). And Psalm 73 says, “Whom have I in heaven but You? And there is none upon earth that I desire besides You” (Psalm 73:25). God does not confront our idols to leave us empty. Paul rejoiced that the Thessalonians had “turned to God from idols to serve the living and true God” (1 Thessalonians 1:9). The old allegiance loses its place so that we can know and enjoy the One who is worth more than all of it. Holiness has not changed between Ekron and Psalm 27. What changes is a heart reconciled through Christ, until the person who once wanted God mainly to solve problems comes to want God Himself.
whole.q: The Philistines wanted their suffering to stop and the ark to leave.

whole.title: Every Rival Will Fall
whole.html: Dagon’s humiliation shows that false religious power cannot stand against the LORD. It belongs to the larger biblical promise that every rival claim to final authority will be overthrown. Christ will deliver the kingdom to the Father “when He puts an end to all rule and all authority and power” (1 Corinthians 15:24). At the last trumpet, voices in heaven announce, “The kingdoms of this world have become the kingdoms of our Lord and of His Christ, and He shall reign forever and ever!” (Revelation 11:15). First Samuel 5 does not describe those future events, but it shows the same reality. No enemy can permanently frustrate God’s purposes.
whole.q: Dagon’s humiliation shows that false religious power cannot stand against the LORD.

whole.title: Not Only That Our Dagons Fall, but That Christ Reigns
whole.html:
If we look only at the destruction of Dagon, our application can become merely negative: find the idols and remove them. But God is after more than an empty room. He calls us to “love the LORD your God with all your heart, with all your soul, with all your mind, and with all your strength” (Mark 12:30). Removing a competing loyalty is never the goal by itself. What fills the place it leaves? The New Testament answers with the life of Jesus Christ. “It is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me” (Galatians 2:20). Paul prayed that Christ would “dwell in your hearts through faith,” so that believers would be “rooted and grounded in love” (Ephesians 3:17). Holiness is not mainly a list of things we no longer do. It is a life increasingly filled with the knowledge, love and presence of Christ, because He has become the One we love and trust most.

1 Samuel 5. The glory that “departed from Israel” was never defeated. With no Israelite army, priest or prophet acting on His behalf, the LORD humbles Dagon in his own house, breaks the idol’s head and hands, and lays His heavy hand on one Philistine city after another until they beg to send His ark away. God does not need us to defend His honor, and He will not share His place with any rival. Yet the chapter also shows how far people can see His power without surrendering to Him. God wants more than to be recognized. He wants to be known, trusted and loved.

What God may be saying: “I am still God when My people fail, and My help has not ended. I will not share your heart with your idols, but I am not taking them away to leave you empty. Let them fall before Me, and do not set them up again. Do not send Me away to keep what is breaking you. Humble yourself under My hand, and come to Me for Myself.”
whole.q: If we look only at the destruction of Dagon, our application can become merely negative: find the idols and remove them.

1.brief: The Philistines take the captured ark of God and bring it from Ebenezer to Ashdod. The ark now enters Philistine territory as a prize of war.
1.explain:
“Then the Philistines took the ark of God”

Chapter 4 ended with a dying mother's cry that the glory had departed from Israel. Chapter 5 follows the ark itself. “The Philistines took the ark of God” as plunder from the battlefield. To them it was a prize of war, the captured emblem of a defeated people's god. The narrator still calls it “the ark of God.” Its capture had not changed whose ark it was.

“and brought it from Ebenezer to Ashdod.”

The Philistines carried the ark from “Ebenezer,” the Israelite camp where it had been taken (4:1), to “Ashdod,” one of their five principal cities (6:17). Ashdod lay on the coastal plain, several miles inland from the Mediterranean, well inside Philistine territory. From a human point of view, the ark was now as far from Israel's help as it could be. No Israelite army, priest, or prophet went with it. Whatever happened next, Israel would have no part in it.
1.notes:
Ashdod is identified with Tel Ashdod (Esdud), about three to four miles (5–6 km) inland from the coast.

The five Philistine cities were Ashdod, Gaza, Ashkelon, Gath, and Ekron (Joshua 13:3; 1 Samuel 6:17).

Gaza also had a temple of Dagon, where the Philistine lords offered sacrifice after Samson's capture (Judges 16:23).

The account of the ark itself runs from 4:1 to 7:2, within the larger movement of the ark, the LORD's judgment, and Israel's return to the LORD that continues through 7:17. In chapter 5 no Israelite speaks or acts.

hearing.observe: Israel had just lost thirty thousand soldiers, the priests Hophni and Phinehas were dead, and the ark was gone (4:10–11). It looked as though Israel’s God had been beaten along with Israel. But Israel had lost because God had allowed judgment to fall on a disobedient and presumptuous people, not because God had grown weak. Psalm 78 says plainly that He “delivered His strength into captivity, and His glory into the enemy’s hand” (Psalm 78:61). God was disciplining His people, and He had not stopped being their God. Hebrews says the Father disciplines those He loves, and does it for their good (Hebrews 12:6, 10).
hearing.hear: God may let me experience defeat because of my own disobedience or spiritual drift. But my failure does not make Him smaller. Israel’s sin cost them the battle and the ark; it did not weaken the LORD at all. My sin can cost me peace with Him and the joy of His blessing, yet He is still as strong and faithful as He was before I failed. When He disciplines me, He has not abandoned me; He is still claiming me as His own. So I don’t have to hide my defeat from Him. I can bring it to Him honestly, confess what caused it, and trust Him to restore me.

hearing.observe: The ark is carried away from Ebenezer, a name that means “stone of help.” Israel had camped there and lost (4:1), so the place of their defeat carried a name that promised help. They had tried to force God’s help by carrying the ark into battle like a good-luck charm (4:3). His help did not come their way. But it had not ended. In chapter 7, after Israel repents, Samuel will set up a stone of victory and give it this same name: “Ebenezer, saying, ‘Thus far the LORD has helped us’” (7:12). The road from defeat to that second Ebenezer runs through repentance and trust in the LORD Himself.
hearing.hear: God’s help has not ended just because it did not come the way I tried to force it. I may have treated something holy like a good-luck charm and watched it fail. He may first let my false confidence fail so that I learn to depend on Him. The place where I was defeated may become the place where I can say with Samuel that the LORD has helped me this far.

hearing.observe: The ark was the sign of God’s throne and the place where He promised to meet His people (Exodus 25:22). Now it is seized and carried into enemy territory, where it will humble the enemy’s god. Christians have long seen in this a picture of what happened to Jesus. Jesus was seized, bound and led away (John 18:12). At the cross it looked like the end. Yet there Christ “disarmed principalities and powers” and made “a public spectacle of them, triumphing over them in it” (Colossians 2:15). The ark is not Christ, and this verse is about the capture of the ark. But the pattern is the same: what looks like God’s defeat becomes the place of His victory.
hearing.hear: What looks like God’s defeat in my life may be the very place He is winning. Jesus looked defeated when He was led away, and that was the road to His victory. When God’s cause seems to lose, I do not have to read the outcome from the circumstances. I can read the circumstances in the light of the cross.

reflections.title: Still “the Ark of God.”
reflections.html: The verse could have said “the captured ark” or “the Philistines’ prize.” It says “the ark of God.” The Philistines had taken the object, but they had not taken God, and capture did not change whose it was. The rest of the chapter shows the LORD acting in enemy land with no Israelite helper. People often mistake the outward signs of God’s work for God Himself. When the signs are carried off, it can feel as though God has lost. But His honor does not rise and fall with the fortunes of the things that represent Him. When His people fail and His cause seems to lose, God Himself has not lost. Am I judging God’s strength by how His cause looks today?
reflections.q: Am I judging God’s strength by how His cause looks today?

reflections.title: What We Capture, We Do Not Control
reflections.html: The Philistines possessed the ark, but owning it did not give them authority over the God it represented. They could carry the sacred chest from place to place, choose where it stood, and surround it with their own religious symbols. They could not control what God would do. There is a deep difference between having something associated with God and having authority over God. Israel had already made this mistake by trying to use the ark to win a battle (4:3). Now the Philistines made a similar mistake by treating it as the property of a victorious nation. A church can own buildings, programs and traditions that once carried God’s presence. None of them gives us control over Him. Am I trying to hold on to God through something I possess?
reflections.q: Am I trying to hold on to God through something I possess?

reflections.title: Into Enemy Territory, but Never a Prisoner
reflections.html: The ark goes from Ebenezer into Ashdod, a Philistine stronghold. It looks like captivity. But what follows is not the story of a helpless God locked in a foreign land. It is the story of the LORD asserting His authority there. Jesus followed a deeper version of this pattern. He entered a fallen world, accepted humiliation, and submitted to death. Yet entering our condition did not put Him under the power of evil. Through death He destroyed “him who had the power of death, that is, the devil” (Hebrews 2:14). The ark is not a picture of Christ in every detail, but the movement from apparent captivity to revealed authority points to Him. He came into enemy territory to set captives free.
reflections.q: The ark goes from Ebenezer into Ashdod, a Philistine stronghold.

2.brief: They bring the ark of God into the house of Dagon and set it beside their god. Placing it there presents Israel’s God as though He were a captive trophy in Dagon’s house.
2.explain:
“When the Philistines took the ark of God, they brought it into the house of Dagon”

“The house of Dagon” was Dagon's temple in Ashdod. “Dagon” was a major god of the Philistines, to whom they had offered a great sacrifice when Samson was captured, saying, “Our god has delivered into our hands Samson our enemy!” (Judges 16:23). Bringing the ark into Dagon's temple made the same claim: Dagon had defeated Israel's God.

“and set it by Dagon.”

The Philistines placed the ark “by Dagon,” beside the image of their god. Victorious peoples in the ancient world often placed captured gods or sacred objects in the temple of their own god as trophies, displaying their god's superiority. The ark was set there as a captive, a subordinate beside the conqueror. That is how the scene looked to the Philistines. The next morning would show who was subordinate to whom.
2.notes:
A god named Dagan was worshiped widely in the ancient Near East, including at Mari, Ebla, and Ugarit, long before the Philistines settled in Canaan. The Philistines apparently adopted him after arriving.

Two explanations of the name have been proposed: a connection with the Hebrew word dagan, ‘grain,’ suggesting a god of crops, and a connection with dag, ‘fish,’ which gave rise to the familiar picture of Dagon as half man, half fish. The fish-shaped image comes from later interpretation and is not established, and neither explanation of the name is settled.

After Saul's death the Philistines fastened his head “in the temple of Dagon” (1 Chronicles 10:10), another example of war trophies displayed in their god's house.

hearing.observe: The Philistines had done this kind of thing before. When they captured Samson, they gathered to sacrifice to Dagon, saying, “Our god has delivered into our hands Samson our enemy!” (Judges 16:23). Setting the ark “by Dagon” said that Israel’s God was now one god among many, and the lesser one. But the LORD had said, “My glory I will not give to another, nor My praise to carved images” (Isaiah 42:8). He does not debate Dagon or bargain with him. The arrangement does not last one night. Paul asks the same question about believers: “What agreement has the temple of God with idols? For you are the temple of the living God” (2 Corinthians 6:16).
hearing.hear: God will not share a place in my heart. He does not ask for a spot on the shelf beside my other trusts. He asks for first place, because He alone is God. I don’t want to keep Him beside the things I rely on. Giving Him the whole room is not a loss; it is freedom.

hearing.observe: Nothing in this verse suggests the Philistines meant to give up Dagon. They simply added Israel’s God to the religion they already had. People can do the same with the true God. We welcome Him into our lives and expect Him to fit in alongside everything that already governs us. We want His protection, peace and blessing without giving Him the throne. Some have called this an “additive gospel”: Jesus plus my ambition, plus my comfort, plus my control. But receiving God is not adding one more influence to a life that is already arranged. It means yielding to Him the authority over that life.
hearing.hear: There is a difference between adding God to my life and surrendering my life to God. I can ask Him to bless my plans without ever handing Him my plans. I want to move from wanting God to take part in my life to yielding my life to His rule.

hearing.observe: Dagon stood in the place of honor in his own house, and the ark’s arrival challenged that place. Spurgeon preached this scene as a picture of grace entering a heart and confronting its idols, especially self-righteousness and cherished sin. An idol is not always something obviously evil. It can be something good that has been given a place of ultimate trust. Control, reputation, financial security, success in ministry, personal achievement, and even religious knowledge can become the real authority in a life. The question is not always whether something should stay, but whether it has taken a place that belongs to God alone.
hearing.hear: What sits in the place of honor in my life? It may be a good thing: my family, my work, my reputation, even my ministry. When the Lord comes near, He challenges whatever I have set up in His place. I can let Him show me what I have trusted most, and give that place back to Him.

reflections.title: Success Is Not Approval; Defeat Is Not Rejection
reflections.html: By putting the ark in Dagon’s temple, the Philistines were saying that Dagon had beaten the LORD. They read their military victory as proof that their god was greater. But they misunderstood why Israel lost. Israel was defeated because of God’s judgment on His own people, not because Dagon had grown stronger than the LORD. People often confuse an outcome with an explanation. A thriving business, a growing ministry or a won argument does not prove that God approves. A loss, a closed door or a hard season does not prove that He has rejected us. Success does not necessarily mean divine approval, and defeat does not necessarily mean divine rejection. Am I reading God’s verdict from my results?
reflections.q: Am I reading God’s verdict from my results?

reflections.title: Not One God Among Many
reflections.html: Whatever the Philistines intended, putting the ark beside Dagon placed Israel’s God inside Dagon’s religious world, as one power among several. But the LORD cannot be assigned a place in a collection of gods. He is not one spiritual option among many. “Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God, the LORD is one!” (Deuteronomy 6:4). “You shall have no other gods before Me” (Exodus 20:3). Our culture often treats faith the same way the Philistines did, as one shelf in a large store of beliefs and practices. God does not merely want a place in our lives. He claims the highest place, because He alone is God. Have I given God a place in my life, or the place?
reflections.q: Have I given God a place in my life, or the place?

reflections.title: God Shows Himself Where He Is Least Honored
reflections.html: Dagon’s temple was built to magnify Dagon. It was not a place where the LORD was honored at all. Yet the arrival of the ark made it the stage for Dagon’s humiliation and the LORD’s glory. Scripture often shows God revealing Himself in unexpected places. He met Moses in the wilderness, confronted Pharaoh in Egypt, met Jacob while he was running for his life, and sent His Son into the world in humble circumstances in Bethlehem. God’s authority is not limited to places where people already welcome Him. That does not mean He approves of what happens in a house of false worship. It means there is no territory beyond His rule. Is there a place I have assumed God could never show up?
reflections.q: Is there a place I have assumed God could never show up?

reflections.title: What God’s Presence Reveals About a House
reflections.html: The ark’s arrival exposed what Dagon’s temple was really about. The question was not only which objects were in the room, but which one was honored as supreme. The same is true of churches and homes. A church can have Scripture, songs, spiritual language and many activities, and still be run in practice by something other than the Lord: money, reputation, a personality, or the way things have always been done. The same can be true of an individual believer. When the Lord comes near, He shows what actually governs the house. If God’s presence came fully into my home, church or heart, what would it reveal as the real authority?
reflections.q: If God’s presence came fully into my home, church or heart, what would it reveal as the real authority?

3.brief: Early the next morning the people of Ashdod find Dagon fallen on its face to the earth before the ark of the LORD, and they must set it back in its place. The idol lies prostrate before the LORD and depends on its worshipers to stand again.
3.explain:
“And when the people of Ashdod arose early in the morning,”

The next day began like any other at the temple. The people of Ashdod, likely including Dagon's priests and worshipers, came early, perhaps to offer their morning worship.

“there was Dagon, fallen on its face to the earth before the ark of the LORD.”

What they found was humiliating. Dagon had “fallen on its face to the earth,” the posture of a worshiper bowing down in submission before a superior. The idol lay prostrate “before the ark of the LORD.” The narrator now uses the name “the LORD,” Israel's God by His own name, for the first time in this chapter. The scene reverses the Philistines' intention. They had set the ark beside Dagon as a captive; Dagon now lay facedown before the ark as a servant before his Master. No Israelite was present. The LORD needed no one to defend Him.

“So they took Dagon and set it in its place again.”

The worshipers lifted their god back onto his pedestal. The verse exposes the helplessness of an idol. Dagon could not raise himself; his own people had to set him up again. Isaiah later mocks idols that must be carried and set in place, “a carved image that will not totter” (Isaiah 40:20), and the Psalms describe idols that have hands but cannot handle and feet but cannot walk (Psalm 115:7). The LORD, by contrast, had acted alone in the night.
3.notes:
The Philistines “took” the ark (5:1–2), and now they must “take” Dagon to put him back; the same Hebrew verb is used.

Earlier in this account the Philistines had spoken of the plagues on Egypt (4:8). In 6:6 their priests again recall Egypt as they advise sending the ark back.

hearing.observe: Overnight the whole arrangement was reversed. Dagon is found “fallen on its face to the earth before the ark of the LORD,” the posture of a worshiper bowing low. The NKJV uses the same words for Joshua, who “fell on his face to the earth and worshiped” before the Commander of the LORD’s army (Joshua 5:14). Notice that the narrator now calls it “the ark of the LORD,” using God’s covenant name. The story records no Israelite intervention and no human hand at work. It presents the fall as the LORD’s victory, won without anyone’s help. Dagon could not stand before the true God.
hearing.hear: God will not allow my idols to stand before Him. When I come into His presence, the things I have put in His place start to become uncomfortable, and that discomfort is His mercy. It is not a feeling that does the work for me. His presence exposes the idol; then I respond. I name the trust that has taken His place, confess it to Him, and give that place back to Him. I don’t have to wrestle my idols down in my own strength, but I do have to stop defending them.

hearing.observe: “So they took Dagon and set it in its place again.” The worshipers had to lift their god off the floor. Isaiah later mocks idols in exactly these terms: “They bear it on the shoulder, they carry it and set it in its place, and it stands; from its place it shall not move” (Isaiah 46:7). Against these carried gods the LORD says, “Even to your old age, I am He, and even to gray hairs I will carry you!” (Isaiah 46:4). Dagon needed human help to stand. The LORD needed no help to throw him down. Every false god depends on the people who serve it. The living God is the One His people depend on.
hearing.hear: Whatever I have to keep propping up cannot carry me. Money is not the problem; caring for it well is good stewardship. The problem comes when my sense of safety rests on the balance, or my worth rests on what people think of me. Then I spend my life lifting that thing back into place every morning. The living God is the One who carries me, and He has promised to keep carrying me “even to gray hairs.” I can put that weight down and trust Him.

hearing.observe: The people of Ashdod did not let the fallen image challenge their beliefs. They repaired the visible disorder and set things back the way they had been. We can do the same thing. When God exposes pride, self-reliance, misplaced trust or an unhealthy attachment, we may see that something needs to change and still rush to restore the familiar arrangement. We can be more committed to keeping what we know than to receiving what God is showing us.
hearing.hear: I often try to rebuild what God is tearing down in my life. When He lets a false support fall, my first instinct is to set it back up before anyone notices. I want to learn to leave on the floor what God has thrown down, and to ask Him what He is showing me instead.

reflections.title: Every Knee Will Bow, but Not Every Bow Is Love
reflections.html: Dagon lies on his face before the ark, the posture of worship and surrender. But a carved image cannot worship. Its position shows the LORD’s supremacy, but no heart is bowing. This is a small early picture of what Scripture promises: “at the name of Jesus every knee should bow… and that every tongue should confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father” (Philippians 2:10–11). One day every power will bow before Him, willingly or not. There is a difference between acknowledging God because it has become undeniable and worshiping Him because we know and love Him. God does not want us to wait until we have no choice. Am I bowing to Jesus gladly now, or only yielding when I am forced?
reflections.q: Am I bowing to Jesus gladly now, or only yielding when I am forced?

4.brief: The following morning Dagon has fallen again before the ark, and its head and both palms lie broken off on the threshold, leaving only its torso. The second fall is a decisive humiliation, and the idol’s severed hands stand in contrast to the powerful hand of the LORD that follows.
4.explain:
“And when they arose early the next morning, there was Dagon, fallen on its face to the ground before the ark of the LORD.”

The second morning repeated the first, but with a decisive difference. Dagon had again fallen facedown before the ark. The repetition ruled out accident. Whatever the Philistines thought on the first day, the second fall showed that a power greater than Dagon was at work.

“The head of Dagon and both the palms of its hands were broken off on the threshold;”

This time the idol was broken. Its “head” and “both the palms of its hands” lay severed “on the threshold,” the entrance to the inner shrine. In ancient warfare victors sometimes cut off the heads and hands of defeated enemies as proof of victory (compare 17:51; 31:9). Dagon now lay like a defeated warrior. His head, the seat of authority, and his hands, the instruments of power, were gone. The god credited with capturing the ark had no head to rule and no hands to act. The chapter's next section speaks repeatedly of the LORD's hand (5:6, 7, 9, 11), and the contrast is deliberate: Dagon's hands lay broken on the floor while the LORD's hand fell heavy on the city.

“only Dagon's torso was left of it.”

All that remained was the trunk of the image. The god who seemed to have triumphed over Israel's God was reduced to a stump.
4.notes:
The final clause reads literally ‘only Dagon was left to him,’ which is difficult. Translations supply a word such as ‘torso’ or ‘trunk’ to make sense of it (NKJV, NLT).

Some older interpreters connected the phrase with a supposed fish-shaped lower body, but that reading depends on an uncertain explanation of Dagon's name and is not required by the text.

The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament, supplies ‘the back’ or ‘spine’ of Dagon. NETS, the New English Translation of the Septuagint, renders it ‘only the spine of Dagon was left.’

hearing.observe: The first fall could be explained away, and the Philistines simply set Dagon back up. The second fall could not be explained away. An image that has fallen can be lifted. An image with its head and hands broken off cannot be fixed by standing it up again. The first morning was a warning; the second was full exposure. The text does not give a rule that God always works in two stages. But it does show a pattern found elsewhere in Scripture: when people ignore God’s first, gentler warning and keep propping up what He has toppled, His dealings with them can become plainer and more severe.
hearing.hear: When I ignore the Lord’s gentle warnings, His dealings with me can become plainer. He does not shout first. He often begins with a quiet tap on the shoulder. I would rather listen to the first fall than wait for the second. If He is showing me something today, I want to respond while His warning is still gentle.

hearing.observe: The parts broken off were the head and the hands. The head stands for thinking, direction and authority; the hands stand for action, strength and power. These are natural pictures, not hidden meanings in the Hebrew words. Without them Dagon had no mind to rule and no hands to act, which is all an idol ever really was. The psalmist says idols have hands “but they do not handle,” and that “those who make them are like them; so is everyone who trusts in them” (Psalm 115:7–8). Before the LORD, the claimed wisdom and power of a false god lay in pieces on the floor.
hearing.hear: The idols of my own wisdom and my own strength cannot stand before God. I can trust my understanding and my ability until they quietly become my god. Before Him, they fall. I want to take God at His word: “Trust in the LORD with all your heart, and lean not on your own understanding” (Proverbs 3:5).

hearing.observe: “Only Dagon’s torso was left of it.” The head and hands were gone, but the stump of the image still lay in the temple. Spurgeon used this detail as a picture of the believer’s life after Christ has come in. Sin’s authority is broken, but some of the old life remains, and the believer still has to resist it. That is an application, not the meaning of the verse. But it fits the New Testament. Paul tells believers that “sin shall not have dominion over you” (Romans 6:14), and also calls them to “put to death the deeds of the body” by the Spirit (Romans 8:13).
hearing.hear: The old master in my life has been dethroned, even if some remnant of it is still lying around. I don’t have to be discouraged that I still struggle. Sin no longer has the right to rule me. I can keep putting to death by the Spirit what Christ has already broken, and look forward to the day when nothing of it is left.

reflections.title: No Head to Rule, No Hands to Act
reflections.html: In the ancient world, a victor would sometimes cut off the head of a defeated enemy and display it as proof of victory. David did this with Goliath (17:51, 54), and the Philistines later did it to Saul (31:9). First Chronicles adds where his head ended up: they “fastened his head in the temple of Dagon” (1 Chronicles 10:10). Chronicles does not say it was this same building in Ashdod, but the irony is sharp. The Philistines hung their trophy before a god whose own image had once lain headless before the ark. False confidence can outlive the evidence that exposed it. Now Dagon lies like a beaten warrior in his own house, his head and his hands broken off on the threshold. The god who supposedly beat Israel’s God has no head to rule and no hands to act. Without the honor his worshipers gave him, Dagon was only a carved image, which is all he ever really was. Whatever is raised up against God is left without authority or power in His presence.
reflections.q: In the ancient world, a victor would sometimes cut off the head of a defeated enemy and display it as proof of victory.

reflections.title: Hannah’s Song Begins to Come True
reflections.html: Before the ark was ever lost, Hannah sang, “Talk no more so very proudly” and “The adversaries of the LORD shall be broken in pieces” (2:3, 10). She praised the God who “brings low and lifts up” (2:7). In Dagon’s temple the first adversary lies broken in pieces. Dagon had been honored as the victor, and by morning he was on the floor. What people exalt may be what God brings low. Hannah’s song is not an isolated poem. It is a key to the whole book of 1 Samuel. The proud are humbled, the mighty are brought down, and the LORD reverses human expectations. The reversals Hannah sang about are being acted out before our eyes.
reflections.q: Before the ark was ever lost, Hannah sang, “Talk no more so very proudly” and “The adversaries of the LORD shall be broken in pieces” (2:3, 10).

reflections.title: The Powers Stripped of Their Authority
reflections.html: Many Christians have seen in the headless, handless idol a picture of what Christ has done to the powers opposed to Him. At the cross Christ “disarmed principalities and powers” (Colossians 2:15). Jesus described His work the same way: “When a strong man, fully armed, guards his own palace, his goods are in peace. But when a stronger than he comes upon him and overcomes him, he takes from him all his armor in which he trusted” (Luke 11:21–22). Dagon’s temple looked like a stronghold, yet its god lay broken. Satan and sin can look towering. But for the believer who stands in Christ, they are disarmed powers with no right to rule. The comparison is a spiritual picture, not the meaning of the verse. Yet it opens a rich line of meditation on Christ’s supremacy.
reflections.q: Many Christians have seen in the headless, handless idol a picture of what Christ has done to the powers opposed to Him.

reflections.title: A Broken Head
reflections.html: Some Christians have connected Dagon’s broken head with the first promise of the gospel, that the woman’s Seed would crush the serpent’s head (Genesis 3:15). Dagon is not the serpent, and this verse is not a prophecy of the cross. But the scene does fit the larger story of Scripture, in which every power that claims independence from God is finally brought under His rule. Christ “must reign till He has put all enemies under His feet” (1 Corinthians 15:25).
reflections.q: Some Christians have connected Dagon’s broken head with the first promise of the gospel, that the woman’s Seed would crush the serpent’s head (Genesis 3:15).

reflections.title: Broken Hands and the Heavy Hand
reflections.html: Dagon loses both hands in verse 4. Starting in verse 6, the narrative keeps speaking of “the hand of the LORD” (vv. 6, 7, 9, 11). The contrast is striking. The Philistine god is shown without hands. The God of Israel shows that His hand is powerful throughout the Philistine cities. Dagon cannot even protect his own image, while the LORD exercises authority over a whole nation. The chapter communicates its central message through a physical detail rather than a speech. Every human power is a pair of broken hands beside the hand of God.
reflections.q: Dagon loses both hands in verse 4.

reflections.title: The Enemy’s Stronghold Becomes the Place of His Defeat
reflections.html: The Philistines placed the ark inside Dagon’s temple, the place where Dagon should have been strongest. Yet that temple became the scene of his destruction. God does not need His enemies to come out of their strongholds before He can overthrow them. The places where human power seems most secure can become the places where its weakness is exposed. Scripture follows this pattern again and again: Pharaoh was defeated in Egypt, Goliath fell on the battlefield he had dominated, and Christ won His victory through the cross, the very place where evil seemed to win.
reflections.q: The Philistines placed the ark inside Dagon’s temple, the place where Dagon should have been strongest.

reflections.title: Not a Contest Between Equals
reflections.html: The Bible is not describing the LORD as one powerful god who barely defeats another equally real god. Dagon is an idol. His inability to stand exposes the emptiness of everything claimed for him. The LORD does not win because He has more strength within the same category. He is the living Creator, and Dagon is a thing that was made. Isaiah makes this distinction explicit: “To whom will you liken Me, and make Me equal and compare Me, that we should be alike?” (Isaiah 46:5). God does not merely compete with idols. He exposes their nothingness.
reflections.q: The Bible is not describing the LORD as one powerful god who barely defeats another equally real god.

reflections.title: Fixing the Statue or Surrendering the Trust
reflections.html: After the first fall, the Philistines stood Dagon back up, as if the problem were where the statue was standing. The next morning showed that the problem was what the statue claimed to be. Dagon was more than an object in a temple. He stood for the trust of the Philistine people, and his fall struck at the foundation of their confidence. We often do the same thing the Philistines did. We repair the outward disorder and leave the trust underneath untouched. A man may promise his family again and again that he will work fewer hours. He changes his schedule, and within months the long hours are back, because his sense of worth depends on being needed at work. God is not only after the schedule. He is after the place where the man finds his worth. The God who overthrows what we are trying to preserve is not being cruel; He is reaching for the trust underneath. When God exposes an idol, the question is not just what habit needs to change, but what I have been trusting, loving or fearing that only God should hold.
reflections.q: After the first fall, the Philistines stood Dagon back up, as if the problem were where the statue was standing.

reflections.title: When the Idol Gets Set Up Again
reflections.html: The Philistines set Dagon back in his place (v. 3), and the next morning he was down again, this time broken (v. 4). Spurgeon saw in this a struggle many new believers know. Christ comes in, an old sin falls, and then old companions, old habits and the enemy of our souls work hard to set it back up. Sometimes, for a season, they seem to succeed, and the young believer wonders whether his faith was ever real. Spurgeon’s counsel was to grieve over the fall but not to doubt the Lord. The God who threw the idol down once can throw it down again, and often more thoroughly the second time. Many who wandered and came back have come back humbler, more tender and more grateful. That is no excuse for sin: “let him who thinks he stands take heed lest he fall” (1 Corinthians 10:12). But it is hope for the one who has fallen. What the Lord has begun to break, He is able to finish.
reflections.q: The Philistines set Dagon back in his place (v. 3), and the next morning he was down again, this time broken (v. 4).

reflections.title: The Stump Will Not Remain Forever
reflections.html: Only the torso of Dagon was left. Spurgeon used that detail for the sin that still remains in a believer. Its reign is broken, but the old nature has not yet been removed. He warned that this remnant is not dead stone. It can spring back to life when temptation comes near, so the believer must stay watchful and keep away from what feeds it. Paul knew the struggle: “O wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death? I thank God—through Jesus Christ our Lord!” (Romans 7:24–25). And the struggle has an end. The stump of Dagon stayed in the Philistine temple, but the remnant of sin will not stay in God’s people forever. “We know that when He is revealed, we shall be like Him, for we shall see Him as He is” (1 John 3:2). The Lord who dethroned sin in me will one day remove it completely.
reflections.q: Only the torso of Dagon was left.

5.brief: For this reason the priests of Dagon and all who enter his house do not tread on the threshold of Dagon in Ashdod to the writer’s day. The lasting custom preserves the memory of Dagon’s humiliation before the LORD.
5.explain:
“Therefore neither the priests of Dagon nor any who come into Dagon's house”

The narrator explains a custom that resulted from these events. “Therefore” links the practice directly to the breaking of Dagon on the threshold. It applied to “the priests of Dagon” and to all worshipers who entered his temple.

“tread on the threshold of Dagon in Ashdod to this day.”

Dagon's worshipers would not step on the threshold where their god's head and hands had fallen. Perhaps they regarded the spot as sacred or as touched by misfortune. Whatever their reason, they continued the custom “to this day,” meaning up to the time when the account was written. Every time a Philistine stepped over that threshold, the custom bore unwitting witness to the night Dagon fell before the LORD. The worshipers kept a reminder of their god's humiliation as part of his worship.
5.notes: Zephaniah 1:9 speaks of punishing “those who leap over the threshold.” Some interpreters connect that verse with a pagan custom like the one at Ashdod, but the connection is uncertain.

hearing.observe: The priests of Dagon knew exactly what had happened. Their god had fallen twice and been broken in his own house. That should have led them to question him. Instead, they made up a new religious custom around the place of his defeat and went on worshiping him. They had clear evidence of the LORD’s power, and they built religion around something else. An encounter with God’s power does not guarantee a changed heart. People can adjust their practices rather than surrender their beliefs. Seeing is not the same as surrendering.
hearing.hear: I can see God’s power and still not surrender to Him. I can hear a strong sermon, feel His presence in worship, or watch Him answer prayer, and then go on living the same way. What matters is not only what He shows me, but whether I bow to Him because of it.

hearing.observe: Every worshiper who came into Dagon’s house had to step carefully over the very spot where Dagon’s head and hands had fallen. They walked over the evidence of their god’s defeat and kept right on worshiping him. Centuries later the prophet Zephaniah condemned people in Judah who “leap over the threshold” (Zephaniah 1:9). Some think this was the same custom spreading into Judah, though that cannot be proven. Either way, the picture is striking: a threshold-leaper is someone who steps around what God has brought down rather than looking at it.
hearing.hear: I can become a threshold-leaper. I can step carefully around what God has brought down in my life, or around something that has clearly stopped bearing fruit, so that I can keep my life arranged around it. I would rather stop at the threshold, look honestly at what God has done, and let it turn me to Him.

hearing.observe: The same events that hardened the Philistines could have opened their hearts. Scripture shows that people respond very differently to the same kind of evidence. Pharaoh saw plague after plague and hardened his heart. Rahab only heard reports of what the LORD had done at the Red Sea, and she said, “The LORD your God, He is God in heaven above and on earth beneath” (Joshua 2:11). The difference is not always how much evidence a person receives. It is how the heart responds to it.
hearing.hear: The same truth that softens one heart can harden another, and the difference is my response. God has shown me enough of Himself to trust Him. I don’t want to wait for more proof while my heart grows harder. I want to respond like Rahab, with faith, to what He has already shown me.

reflections.title: Keeping the Memory, Explaining Away the Meaning
reflections.html: The threshold custom kept the memory of Dagon’s fall alive “to this day.” But the text gives no sign that Dagon’s worshipers ever abandoned him. They remembered the event and built a practice around it, and the practice let them go on worshiping the god who had fallen. That is how error survives. People do not always give up a false belief when they meet evidence against it. Often they reinterpret the evidence so the belief can continue, and a tradition grows up to protect it. Jesus warned the religious leaders of His day that they were “making the word of God of no effect through your tradition” (Mark 7:13). Churches can do this too. We can celebrate the anniversary of a revival every year while resisting the very repentance that started it. Many traditions are good gifts. The question is whether a tradition helps us obey what God has shown us or shields us from it.
reflections.q: The threshold custom kept the memory of Dagon’s fall alive “to this day.”

reflections.title: Careful, Familiar and Unchanged
reflections.html: Dagon’s priests were careful. They watched where they stepped and kept the custom faithfully. Their practice was precise and familiar, and their understanding of God was completely wrong. Precision is not the same as discernment, and familiarity is not the same as faithfulness. Jesus told the Pharisees that they tithed even their garden herbs but “neglected the weightier matters of the law: justice and mercy and faith” (Matthew 23:23). Something can feel spiritually safe simply because we have always done it. Religious practice is good when it serves submission to God; it becomes dangerous when it replaces it. The real measure of a practice is not how long it has lasted, but whether it agrees with God’s Word and whether we stay teachable when His Word corrects us.
reflections.q: Dagon’s priests were careful.

6.brief: The hand of the LORD is heavy on the people of Ashdod; He ravages them and strikes them with tumors, both the city and its territory. The LORD Himself is the agent of this judgment, acting without any Israelite army.
6.explain:
“But the hand of the LORD was heavy on the people of Ashdod,”

The LORD now turned from Dagon to Dagon's people. “The hand of the LORD” is a common biblical expression for God's active power, whether in deliverance or in judgment. It recalls the plagues on Egypt, where “the hand of the LORD” brought pestilence (Exodus 9:3). “Heavy” comes from the same Hebrew root as ‘glory’ and ‘honor,’ the root that runs through the previous chapter (2:29–30; 4:18, 21–22). Phinehas's wife had cried that the glory had departed from Israel. The LORD's glory had not been diminished; it now rested with crushing weight on the Philistines. Dagon's hands lay broken on the threshold, but the LORD's hand was heavy on Ashdod.

“and He ravaged them and struck them with tumors,”

The verse names the LORD as the agent. “He ravaged them” describes devastation, the kind of destruction that leaves a place desolate. “Struck them with tumors” describes a painful affliction of swellings. Verse 11 adds that many died. Chapter 6 also mentions rats that ravaged the land (6:4–5), which suggests a widespread plague. Scripture does not give a medical diagnosis. What it stresses is that the LORD Himself struck them.

“both Ashdod and its territory.”

The judgment was not limited to the temple or to the city. It reached the surrounding villages and countryside, the whole region around Ashdod. The Philistines had taken the ark as a trophy; it had brought the LORD's judgment into their land.
6.notes:
The word for “tumors” appears in the written Hebrew text as 'ophalim, a word meaning swellings or mounds, also used among the curses of Deuteronomy 28:27 (“the boils of Egypt, with tumors”).

When the passage was read aloud, the Jewish scribal reading tradition directed readers to say a different Hebrew word, techorim, possibly because it was regarded as a less blunt term for the same affliction. Its exact meaning is also uncertain, so “tumors” remains a fair rendering.

The KJV's ‘emerods’ (hemorrhoids) reflects one older interpretation. Modern translations generally render “tumors,” leaving the exact nature open.

The Septuagint adds at this point that mice (or rats) sprang up in the land and that there was a great deathly confusion in the city. The Hebrew text followed by the NKJV does not mention the rats until 6:4–5.

Because of the tumors, the deaths, and the rats of 6:4–5, many interpreters have suggested bubonic plague. That is a possibility, not a proven conclusion.

hearing.observe: The first five verses deal with Dagon in his temple. In verse 6 the scene moves outside the temple to the people who trusted in Dagon. God dealt with the false god first, and then with its hold on the people. The LORD had done the same in Egypt: “Against all the gods of Egypt I will execute judgment: I am the LORD” (Exodus 12:12). What people worship shapes more than their religious practice. It shapes how they see the world and what they build their lives on. So when God confronts an idol, He is also confronting the trust placed in it.
hearing.hear: When God confronts what I trust in place of Him, He deals with the false god first and then with its hold on my life. It is not enough for an idol to fall in principle. If I admit that I have trusted my career for my identity, the next step is to change the decisions that trust has been making: how I spend my evenings, what I say yes to, where I turn when I am afraid. I want my repentance to reach my calendar and my choices, not only my feelings.

hearing.observe: Dagon could not prevent his own fall, and now he could not protect the people of Ashdod either. They trusted in a god who could not give them the protection they needed. This is the false promise of every idol. People turn to idols because they believe the idols can provide something essential: security, identity, peace, satisfaction, success or control. Sooner or later, whatever replaces God as the source of life shows that it cannot give what only God can give.
hearing.hear: I turn to idols because I believe they can give me something I need. Money promises security, approval promises worth, control promises peace. But what cannot protect itself cannot protect me. I can bring my real needs to the God who actually meets them.

hearing.observe: The NKJV says the LORD struck the Philistines “with tumors.” The older King James Version called them “emerods,” meaning hemorrhoids, and many commentators think these were painful swellings in the groin or the rear of the body. The text does not let us be sure, and we should not assume that every tumor here was a hemorrhoid. What is clear is that God’s dealing with the Philistines was intensely personal, painful and impossible to ignore. They could not sit comfortably with the ark among them. This was a specific judgment on Philistia, and it does not mean that every illness or discomfort is God’s punishment.
hearing.hear: God knows how to make me uncomfortable when He is pursuing me. When I am clinging to something He is confronting, He may let me lose my comfort until I pay attention. That discomfort is not proof that He has rejected me. It can be His way of getting my attention so that I will turn to Him.

reflections.title: The Hand That Struck Egypt
reflections.html: “The hand of the LORD” is the language of the Exodus. Moses warned Pharaoh that “the hand of the LORD will be on your cattle” (Exodus 9:3). In the preceding chapter, the Philistines had remembered “the hand of these mighty gods… who struck the Egyptians with all the plagues” (4:8). Now they feel that same hand. The God who rescued His people from Egypt is still the same God, and He goes into enemy territory by Himself.
reflections.q: “The hand of the LORD” is the language of the Exodus.

reflections.title: The Same Glory: Delight or Lament
reflections.html: The ark stood for the LORD’s presence among His people, and His presence is always holy. Yet in Ashdod it brought devastating judgment. Years later, the ark stayed in the house of Obed-Edom, “and the LORD blessed Obed-Edom and all his household” (2 Samuel 6:11). The same ark brought judgment in one house and blessing in another. The ark had no power of its own that changed with its surroundings. It pointed to the holy God, and what changed was how people stood before Him. To those who come to Him by His grace, His glory is something to enjoy. To those who oppose Him, the same glory becomes something to lament. God’s nearness is never neutral. Ashdod’s answer to God’s hand was to get the ark out of town. Scripture also shows what it looks like to welcome His hand. Ezra arrived in Jerusalem “according to the good hand of his God upon him,” and the next verse explains what kind of man he was: “For Ezra had prepared his heart to seek the Law of the LORD, and to do it, and to teach statutes and ordinances in Israel” (Ezra 7:9–10). The order matters. Ezra sought God’s word, then lived it, then taught it. That is not a promise that everyone who studies the Bible will have an easy road. It is a picture of the right response to God’s rule: setting the heart on His word instead of pushing His presence away. For anyone who teaches, the question is pointed: am I doing what I am about to teach? And for all of us: what kind of home am I preparing for His presence?
reflections.q: And for all of us: what kind of home am I preparing for His presence?

reflections.title: The Effects Spread Beyond the Temple
reflections.html: The affliction reached “both Ashdod and its territory.” The text deliberately widens the scope: the consequences were no longer limited to one building or one group of priests. What governs the spiritual life of a community influences the rest of its life. A church’s spiritual condition affects its families. A leader’s choices affect those under his care. A society’s ultimate trust shapes its institutions and moral direction. The specific disease in this passage should not become an explanation for every community’s suffering. But the principle stands: what we worship does not stay inside the sanctuary. It shapes our homes, our health and our life together.
reflections.q: The affliction reached “both Ashdod and its territory.”

reflections.title: What Human Strength Cannot Protect
