reflections.html: The Philistines had just proved their strength. They defeated Israel, captured the ark, carried it across their land and called their rulers together. They could not stop the affliction. Human strength is real, but it has limits, whether it belongs to a person or a nation. A family can do everything right financially and still be undone by one diagnosis. A powerful nation can have the strongest military and economy in the world and still depend entirely on God for its continued existence. Nebuchadnezzar learned this the hard way, confessing that God “does according to His will in the army of heaven and among the inhabitants of the earth. No one can restrain His hand” (Daniel 4:35). Planning, savings and strength are good gifts. But security built on human ability alone is fragile, for individuals and for nations, including our own.
reflections.q: The Philistines had just proved their strength.

reflections.title: Holiness Makes Access Through Christ Precious
reflections.html: Ashdod’s experience shows that sinful people cannot presume on the presence of a holy God. Yet the New Testament says believers have “access by one Spirit to the Father” through Christ (Ephesians 2:18). “Having boldness to enter the Holiest by the blood of Jesus… let us draw near with a true heart in full assurance of faith” (Hebrews 10:19, 22). Those who were once far off “have been brought near by the blood of Christ” (Ephesians 2:13). God’s holiness has not become less serious. Christ has done what sinners could never do for themselves. The God from whom the Philistines wanted distance invites us to draw near through His Son. Do I take that access for granted?
reflections.q: Do I take that access for granted?

reflections.title: A Specific Judgment, Not a General Rule
reflections.html: The text clearly names the LORD as the One who struck Ashdod, so we can speak confidently about God’s judgment in this event. But Scripture does not let us assume that illness in general points to a particular person’s sin. Job’s suffering, Jesus’ words about the man born blind (John 9:1–3), and His answer about the tower of Siloam (Luke 13:1–5) all warn against that conclusion. This chapter teaches us about God’s holiness and authority, not how to explain the sufferings of others.
reflections.q: The text clearly names the LORD as the One who struck Ashdod, so we can speak confidently about God’s judgment in this event.

7.brief: The men of Ashdod recognize that the hand of the God of Israel is harsh against them and against Dagon their god, and they insist that His ark must not remain with them. Their answer is to send the ark away, even as they go on calling Dagon their god.
7.explain:
“And when the men of Ashdod saw how it was, they said,”

The people of Ashdod drew the obvious conclusion. They had seen their god fall twice and break, and now their city was struck with disease and death. They understood that these events were connected.

“The ark of the God of Israel must not remain with us,”

The trophy had become a terror. They called it “the ark of the God of Israel,” acknowledging whose ark it was. Their solution was to send it away. They did not ask what the God of Israel wanted, and they did not turn from their idol to Him. They wanted to be rid of Him.

“for His hand is harsh toward us and Dagon our god.”

They recognized that the God of Israel was behind both the plague on their city and the fall of Dagon. “His hand is harsh” describes severe, unrelenting pressure. Yet they still called Dagon “our god.” They had seen Dagon fall before the LORD, and they continued to claim the broken idol as their own. Their recognition of the LORD's power produced fear but not faith.
7.notes:
In 6:5 the Philistine priests and diviners still hope that the LORD “will lighten His hand” from them and from “your gods,” addressing their own people's gods.

“Harsh” translates a word meaning hard or severe. It is a different word from “heavy” in 5:6 and 5:11, though the meaning overlaps.

hearing.observe: When God’s hand presses on people, it is meant to bring them to Him. David knew that pressure: “Day and night Your hand was heavy upon me.” That heaviness led him to confession: “I acknowledged my sin to You… and You forgave the iniquity of my sin” (Psalm 32:4–5). Ashdod felt the same kind of hand, and its only response was to want God gone. The same pressure can drive one person to God and drive another to try to get rid of Him. Peter tells believers what to do: “Humble yourselves under the mighty hand of God, that He may exalt you in due time” (1 Peter 5:6). James says the same: “Humble yourselves in the sight of the Lord, and He will lift you up” (James 4:10).
hearing.hear: When God’s hand is heavy on me, it is meant to bring me home, not to make me want Him gone. I can humble myself under His mighty hand instead of trying to slip out from under it. When I do, He promises to lift me up in His time.

hearing.observe: The men of Ashdod read the situation exactly right: “His hand is harsh toward us and Dagon our god.” They knew the God of Israel had beaten their god. But their conclusion was that the ark must go, not that Dagon must go. They wanted God’s presence removed rather than their idol. The people of the Gadarenes did the same after Jesus delivered a man from demons: they “began to plead with Him to depart from their region” (Mark 5:17). Faced with holiness, the human heart often asks God to leave instead of asking Him to forgive.
hearing.hear: When God’s presence exposes something I cherish, I face a choice: give up the idol, or try to push God away. I can tell myself I am just changing the subject, or staying busy, or keeping a distance for a while. I don’t want to send the Lord away to keep my idol. I want to let the idol go and keep the Lord.

hearing.observe: Even after finding Dagon facedown and broken, the men of Ashdod still call him “Dagon our god.” Their loyalty outlasted every proof that he was empty. An idol does not always lose its hold when its weakness is shown. People can keep trusting something that has disappointed them again and again, because the issue is deeper than information. It is a matter of love, habit, fear and identity. The psalmist says of idols, “Those who make them are like them; so is everyone who trusts in them” (Psalm 115:8).
hearing.hear: I can cling to something long after it has failed me. A habit, a relationship, a way of coping or a source of comfort can keep calling itself “mine” even when it has let me down many times. I can bring these things to the Lord honestly and ask Him to loosen their hold on my heart.

reflections.title: Two Outsiders, Two Responses
reflections.html: The men of Ashdod call the LORD “the God of Israel,” and they still call Dagon “our god.” They recognize His power, but they will not claim Him. Ruth, another outsider, said to Naomi, “Your people shall be my people, and your God, my God” (Ruth 1:16). Scripture tells of other Gentiles who answered God’s self-revelation with faith. Rahab sided with His people (Joshua 2). Nineveh repented at Jonah’s preaching (Jonah 3). Naaman confessed, “Now I know that there is no God in all the earth, except in Israel” (2 Kings 5:15). All of them encountered the truth about Israel’s God. One response sought distance; the others embraced belonging. Powerful experiences do not automatically produce faith. The right response to revelation is humble trust.
reflections.q: The men of Ashdod call the LORD “the God of Israel,” and they still call Dagon “our god.”

reflections.title: Afraid of God’s Hand Is Not the Fear of the LORD
reflections.html: The people of Ashdod feared the effects of God’s power. But the chapter never shows the reverent submission Scripture calls the fear of the LORD. “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom” (Proverbs 9:10). A mature fear of God is more than wanting to escape punishment. It recognizes His holiness, honors His authority, and responds in reverence. The Philistines recognized danger, but they did not show wisdom.
reflections.q: The people of Ashdod feared the effects of God’s power.

reflections.title: Nearness Without Authority
reflections.html: The ark stood right beside Dagon, but being near did not mean being in harmony. When the men of Ashdod felt God’s hand, they admitted His power, but they did not want Him among them on the terms His holiness required. Believers can do something similar. We want God’s nearness while resisting His authority over particular areas of our lives. We welcome His comfort but push back on His correction. We ask for His power in a crisis while keeping our money, our relationships or our ambitions under our own management. Drawing near to God can feel as though it threatens something we consider essential. But intimacy with God cannot be separated from allegiance to Him. Before I ask how near God feels, I need to ask who is reigning. Paul came to “count all things loss for the excellence of the knowledge of Christ Jesus my Lord” (Philippians 3:8). Maturity means coming to love God as He really is, until He is worth more to me than whatever I am afraid to lose.
reflections.q: The ark stood right beside Dagon, but being near did not mean being in harmony.

8.brief: They gather all the lords of the Philistines to ask what to do with the ark of the God of Israel, and the council decides to carry it to Gath. Relocating the ark carries the crisis into another Philistine city.
8.explain:
“Therefore they sent and gathered to themselves all the lords of the Philistines,”

Ashdod could not decide the matter alone. The people summoned “all the lords of the Philistines,” the rulers of the five cities who together governed the Philistine confederation (Joshua 13:3). Their council made decisions affecting all Philistia.

“and said, ‘What shall we do with the ark of the God of Israel?’”

The question shows the depth of their problem. The ark was too dangerous to keep, yet returning it would mean admitting defeat. They still speak of it as “the ark of the God of Israel.”

“And they answered, ‘Let the ark of the God of Israel be carried away to Gath.’”

The lords decided to move the ark to “Gath,” another of the five cities, farther inland. Perhaps they thought the troubles in Ashdod were local, or that they could test whether the ark itself was the cause. Either way, they were trying to manage the God of Israel by moving His ark. Gath would later be the home of Goliath (17:4).

“So they carried the ark of the God of Israel away.”

The decision was carried out. The phrase “the ark of the God of Israel” appears three times in this verse. The Philistines could not stop speaking of whose ark it was.
8.notes:
“Lords” translates seranim, a term used in the Old Testament only for the Philistine rulers. It is not the ordinary Hebrew word for king or lord and may be a loanword from the Philistines' own language.

Some scholars connect it with the Greek word tyrannos, ‘ruler,’ but the derivation is uncertain.

Gath is commonly identified with Tell es-Safi, inland and east of Ashdod near the edge of the lowland hills facing Judah.

hearing.observe: The Philistine lords never ask what the God of Israel wants. Their question shows what was in their hearts: “What shall we do with the ark?” After everything that had happened, the better question was what they should do in response to the God who had shown His power. They treated Him as a problem to be moved, and their solution was a change of address. Israel had made a similar mistake in chapter 4, when they tried to use the ark to win a battle. Both treated God’s presence as something to handle. But the Philistines’ problem was not geography. They had a problem with God, and the God they were moving is the One who “is a consuming fire” (Hebrews 12:29). Changing circumstances can be wise, but it can never replace responding to Him.
hearing.hear: God is not a problem for me to place where He is convenient. I can keep the Lord in certain rooms of my life, like Sunday mornings or a crisis, and move Him away from the rest. And when trouble comes, I often ask how to change my circumstances when the more important question is how I should respond to God in them. Before I ask, “What should I do about this?” I want to ask, “Lord, what are You doing, and how do You want me to respond?”

hearing.observe: “What shall we do with the ark of the God of Israel?” Centuries later another ruler asked a similar question about Jesus. Pilate said, “What then shall I do with Jesus who is called Christ?” (Matthew 27:22). The ark is not Christ, but the question is the same kind of question. When God comes near, everyone has to decide what to do with Him. There are really only two answers: send Him away, or bow before Him. Moving the question somewhere else does not answer it.
hearing.hear: I have to decide what to do with Jesus, and putting off the decision is a way of sending Him away. I can’t pass Him to another room or another day. The honest answers are only two: send Him away, or bow before Him. I choose to bow.

reflections.title: No Council Can Overrule God
reflections.html: The Philistine lords held real authority over their cities. Their vote could move the ark from Ashdod to Gath. But their vote could not tell God what to do. After the ark was carried to Gath, the LORD’s hand struck there too (5:9). Human leaders can decide many things, but none of their decisions bind the LORD. This matters for those entrusted with responsibility in churches and ministries. A board can vote on a building, a budget or a program. No position, title or vote gives anyone control over the presence, power or purposes of God.
reflections.q: The Philistine lords held real authority over their cities.

reflections.title: Competent but Not Discerning
reflections.html: The Philistine rulers were capable leaders. They gathered, discussed, decided and carried out a plan, and their organization worked. They knew the ark had been captured, that Dagon had fallen and that Ashdod had suffered. Yet their decision was to send the problem to Gath, and it failed, because information alone does not produce discernment. They solved the logistics and missed what God was saying through the whole crisis: that Dagon was no god and that the LORD would not be managed. Leaders can be skilled at solving practical problems while missing the spiritual issue entirely. In Christian ministry, godly leadership requires more than competence. It requires the humility to ask what God is saying and the obedience to act on it.
reflections.q: The Philistine rulers were capable leaders.

reflections.title: God Is Not Local
reflections.html: When the ark went to Gath, the Philistines learned that the LORD’s authority did not stop at the edge of Ashdod. The ancient world often thought of gods as local or territorial powers. The LORD is not confined to one temple, one city or one nation. “The earth is the LORD’s, and all its fullness” (Psalm 24:1). People can move the ark and assign it a place, but they never acquire authority over God. His authority and power are not even contained in one church or one movement. He is Lord of heaven and earth.
reflections.q: When the ark went to Gath, the Philistines learned that the LORD’s authority did not stop at the edge of Ashdod.

9.brief: After the ark is carried to Gath, the hand of the LORD comes against that city with very great destruction, striking its men, small and great, with tumors. Moving the ark does not escape the LORD’s judgment but only extends it.
9.explain:
“So it was, after they had carried it away, that the hand of the LORD was against the city with a very great destruction;”

Moving the ark did not escape the LORD's judgment; it carried the judgment to Gath. “The hand of the LORD” appears again. The narrator states plainly that the LORD was “against the city.” “A very great destruction” describes panic and confusion as well as devastation. The Hebrew word suggests a city thrown into turmoil.

“and He struck the men of the city, both small and great,”

The LORD struck the people of Gath as He had struck Ashdod. “Both small and great” means everyone, young and old, common people and leaders alike. No one was exempt.

“and tumors broke out on them.”

The same affliction appeared in Gath. The repetition confirmed that the ark's presence, and the LORD's hand, not local conditions, was the cause.
9.notes:
The verb translated “broke out” is rare, and its exact meaning is uncertain. Some take it to mean that the tumors burst out on the body; others relate it to swelling.

A similar pattern runs through Ashdod, Gath, and Ekron: the ark arrives and the hand of the LORD weighs heavily on the city. The order is not identical.

At Ashdod the stroke comes first and the people then decide to send the ark away (5:6–8). At Gath only the stroke is recorded (5:9). At Ekron the people cry out as soon as the ark arrives (5:10), before the deadly affliction is described (5:11–12).

hearing.observe: The Philistines thought moving the ark would move the problem. Instead, the same affliction broke out in a second city. That proved the trouble was not a local condition; it was the hand of the LORD. Moving God’s ark did not remove His hand. It only spread it. David asked, “Where can I go from Your Spirit? Or where can I flee from Your presence?” (Psalm 139:7). For the Philistines, that truth was a threat. For God’s children, it is one of the great comforts of Scripture, because the God we cannot escape is the God who never leaves us.
hearing.hear: There is nowhere I can go to get away from God. If I am running from Him, that is a sobering truth. If I belong to Him, it is a deep comfort. Wherever I go, even “the uttermost parts of the sea,” His hand will lead me and hold me (Psalm 139:9–10).

hearing.observe: The Philistines moved the ark but did not change their response to God. So the confrontation followed them to Gath. People can do the same with God’s conviction. We change jobs, churches, relationships or surroundings without dealing with what God is confronting in our hearts. Or we pass the problem to someone else. The Philistine lords solved Ashdod’s problem by handing it to Gath. But we cannot get rid of God’s conviction by moving it somewhere else or putting it on someone else. A change of setting may bring relief, but it cannot do what only repentance can do.
hearing.hear: I cannot get rid of God’s conviction by moving it somewhere else or blaming someone else. If I keep running into the same issue in new places, the issue may be in me. I want to stop passing it along and bring it to the Lord in confession.

hearing.observe: The Philistine leaders tried a solution in Ashdod, and it failed in Gath. They would try it again in Ekron. They kept changing the method without questioning their understanding of the problem. The crisis exposed that they thought they faced a problem of location when they faced the LORD Himself. That gives a principle for discernment: repeated failure may show that we have misunderstood the nature of a problem, not just chosen the wrong way to solve it.
hearing.hear: When I keep failing at the same thing, I may need to ask whether I have understood the problem at all. I can keep trying new methods for something that is really a matter of the heart. I can ask the Lord to show me what is really going on, not just how to fix it.

reflections.title: Both Small and Great, and the Champion of Gath
reflections.html: The LORD struck the men of Gath “both small and great.” Common people and leaders were struck alike, and no rank, gift or connection put anyone beyond God’s reach. The Hebrew word translated “destruction” in this verse also carries the idea of panic and confusion; a strong Philistine city was thrown into turmoil. Gath is also a city with a future in the story. It will be the hometown of Goliath (17:4). The God whose hand fell on Gath here will later raise up a shepherd boy to bring down Gath’s champion. Like Dagon before the ark, Goliath will fall “on his face to the earth” and lose his head (17:49, 51). In chapter 5 the LORD humbles Philistine religion without any Israelite champion. In chapter 17 He defeats Philistine military power through His anointed. Both show that the LORD gives victory by His own purpose, not by human strength.
reflections.q: The LORD struck the men of Gath “both small and great.”

reflections.title: Lord Over Life Itself
reflections.html: The first confrontation in the chapter concerned a carved image. Now the narrative describes God’s judgment on living people. God’s power is not limited to a contest of religious symbols. He has authority over human life itself. Dagon cannot even keep himself standing. The LORD shows His authority over life, health and the affairs of nations.
reflections.q: The first confrontation in the chapter concerned a carved image.

reflections.title: The Body Reminds Us We Depend on God
reflections.html: The LORD’s judgment here included bodily affliction. Human strength, independence and confidence were confronted through the weakness of the body. This passage does not teach that ordinary illness is God’s punishment. But it does remind us that human life depends on God. Physical weakness can expose the illusion that we are self-sufficient. For the believer, that should lead not to fearful guessing about the cause of sickness, but to humility, gratitude and trust.
reflections.q: The LORD’s judgment here included bodily affliction.

reflections.title: Severe, but Not Arbitrary
reflections.html: The narrative presents the affliction as the work of the LORD, whose authority had been openly challenged. His judgment comes in the setting of the Philistines’ treatment of His ark and their loyalty to false worship. God is not acting like a jealous rival trying to gain status. He is the righteous Lord, whose glory cannot be dishonored forever without consequence. Scripture consistently presents His judgments as expressions of His holy character, even when the details of His purposes are beyond our understanding.
reflections.q: The narrative presents the affliction as the work of the LORD, whose authority had been openly challenged.

10.brief: The ark of God is sent on to Ekron, and as it arrives the Ekronites cry out that it has been brought to kill them and their people. Their immediate alarm suggests they already knew what the ark had brought on Ashdod and Gath.
10.explain:
“Therefore they sent the ark of God to Ekron.”

Gath also sent the ark away. “Ekron” was the northernmost of the five Philistine cities, closest to Israelite territory. The ark was moving, city by city, back toward the border.

“So it was, as the ark of God came to Ekron, that the Ekronites cried out, saying,”

The people of Ekron did not wait for the plague to begin. As soon as the ark arrived, they cried out in alarm. They knew what had happened in Ashdod and Gath.

“They have brought the ark of the God of Israel to us, to kill us and our people!”

The Ekronites accused their own leaders of sending death to them. “To kill us and our people” shows that they now understood the ark's presence as deadly. The trophy that the Philistines had carried home in triumph from Ebenezer had become a terror that no Philistine city wanted.
10.notes: Ekron is identified with Tel Miqne, near the border with Judah. The ark later went from there to Beth Shemesh in Israelite territory (6:12–16).

hearing.observe: The people of Ekron were terrified before the text describes any plague reaching them. The news of what the LORD had done had run ahead of His ark. Their alarm shows how hostile powers react when God draws near. Years later Ekron’s god was called Baal-Zebub (2 Kings 1:2), and the Gospels use a similar name, Beelzebub, for the ruler of demons (Matthew 12:24). First Samuel 5 does not mention that god, and the Ekronites here are frightened people, not demons. But the New Testament shows the same reaction in the spiritual realm: demons cried out in fear when Jesus came near (Mark 1:24). James gives believers the right order: “Submit to God. Resist the devil and he will flee from you. Draw near to God and He will draw near to you” (James 4:7–8).
hearing.hear: The best way to deal with the darkness in my life is not to fix my attention on the enemy, but to draw near to God. That does not mean temptation disappears the moment I feel close to Him. Drawing near means submitting to God: confessing what He shows me, obeying what He says, and refusing to make room for the devil. When I do that, I can resist the enemy from a place of nearness to God instead of fear.

hearing.observe: The Ekronites cry, “They have brought the ark of the God of Israel to us.” Throughout the chapter the Philistines keep naming whose ark it is: “the ark of the God of Israel,” three times in verse 8 alone. They speak the right name for God, but they want nothing to do with Him. Their words confess what their hearts refuse. It is possible to use the right language about God, to speak His name accurately and even often, without knowing Him or yielding to Him.
hearing.hear: I can have the right language about God without knowing Him. I can say “Lord” and “God” correctly, sing the right songs and use the right words, and still keep Him at arm’s length. I don’t just want to speak about God accurately. I want to know Him and yield to Him.

reflections.title: Pressure Exposes False Unity
reflections.html: When the ark arrives, the people of Ekron cry out against the leaders who sent it to them. The Philistine league that stood united against Israel begins to come apart under God’s presence. When people try to escape God without repenting, they often end up turning on one another. Guilt and consequences get pushed onto whoever is nearby. A family, a team or a church can look united until pressure comes. Unity built on resisting God does not hold.
reflections.q: When the ark arrives, the people of Ekron cry out against the leaders who sent it to them.

reflections.title: Knowing Enough to Fear, Not Enough to Trust
reflections.html: The Ekronites knew enough about what had happened in Ashdod and Gath to be terrified. But their immediate response was rejection. They saw the ark’s arrival only as a threat. There are people who know a great deal about God and recognize that He is holy and powerful, yet are unwilling to surrender to Him. The problem is not always a lack of information. It may be a heart that does not want the God the information reveals. The same holy God who judges sin also offers reconciliation. Paul says God “has committed to us the word of reconciliation” and pleads, “be reconciled to God” (2 Corinthians 5:19–20). The answer to our distance from God is not to remove Him from our lives. It is to be reconciled to Him.
reflections.q: The Ekronites knew enough about what had happened in Ashdod and Gath to be terrified.

reflections.title: Leaders’ Decisions Fall on Others
reflections.html: The ark came to Ekron because of a decision made by rulers elsewhere, and the people of Ekron protested that it had been brought to them. Decisions made by powerful people affect whole communities, including people who were never consulted. Godly leaders think about those who will have to live with the consequences of what they decide.
reflections.q: The ark came to Ekron because of a decision made by rulers elsewhere, and the people of Ekron protested that it had been brought to them.

11.brief: The lords of the Philistines are gathered again, and the people plead that the ark of the God of Israel be sent back to its own place so that it does not kill them, for deadly destruction fills the city and the hand of God is very heavy there. The repeated judgment forces the Philistines to give up the trophy they had taken.
11.explain:
“So they sent and gathered together all the lords of the Philistines, and said,”

The council of lords met a second time. The people of Ekron now set the agenda.

“Send away the ark of the God of Israel, and let it go back to its own place,”

The demand was clear: return the ark to Israel. “Its own place” meant Israel's land and sanctuary. The Philistines had tried keeping it in Dagon's temple and moving it from city to city. Now they recognized that the ark of the God of Israel belonged with Israel. The trophy they had taken in triumph must be given up.

“so that it does not kill us and our people.”

The motive was survival. The Philistines wanted to be free of the LORD's judgment, not to know Him.

“For there was a deadly destruction throughout all the city;”

The narrator explains their desperation. “Deadly destruction” combines panic with death. People were dying throughout Ekron.

“the hand of God was very heavy there.”

The section ends where it began, with God's heavy hand (5:6). “Very heavy” intensifies the description. Once again the narrator uses the root associated with glory. The glory had departed from Israel (4:21–22), but God's glory had not departed from the world. It weighed upon those who had claimed victory over Him.
11.notes:
“Deadly destruction” is literally ‘a confusion (or panic) of death.’ The same word for confusion appears in 5:9 (“a very great destruction”).

The second council (5:11) parallels the first (5:8): the first moved the ark, and the second demanded its return.

hearing.observe: In Egypt, God said to Pharaoh, “Let My people go” (Exodus 5:1), and Pharaoh refused until God’s hand forced him. Here the Philistines beg, “Send away the ark… let it go back.” The Hebrew verb behind “send away” is the same verb God used in “Let My people go” (shalach, meaning to send off or release). Just as Egypt could not hold God’s people, Philistia could not hold God’s ark. Nothing that belongs to God can be held by His enemies. The New Testament shows the same truth at the empty tomb: God raised Jesus up, “because it was not possible that He should be held by it” (Acts 2:24).
hearing.hear: Nothing that belongs to God can be held by His enemies, and that includes me. If I belong to Christ, no power of sin, death or darkness can keep its grip on me forever. Death could not hold Him, and it will not hold those who are His.

hearing.observe: The word “heavy” from verse 6 returns here, made stronger: “the hand of God was very heavy there.” The longer they kept the ark, the heavier God’s hand became. Yet the Philistines want only one thing: that the ark “does not kill us.” Their goal is survival, not knowing the God who sent the judgment. They wanted relief from the consequences rather than a changed relationship with the One who was confronting them. Their greatest need was not relief but a right relationship with God.
hearing.hear: God wants me to seek Him for Himself, not only for relief from my trouble. I can pray hard for a problem to go away and never seek the One who is speaking through it. I want more than relief. I want Him.

hearing.observe: Even the Philistines recognize that the ark has “its own place.” It belonged among God’s people, and God was bringing it home by His own power. But notice what they do: they give back the ark without giving themselves. They let go of the sacred object because keeping it hurt too much, but they do not turn to the LORD. It is possible to give back something that belongs to God because holding it has become painful, and still not surrender our hearts to Him.
hearing.hear: I can give back to God what belongs to Him and still keep my heart to myself. I may return my time, my gifts or the credit for what He has done simply because holding on has become uncomfortable. The Philistines did exactly that with the ark. The Lord wants more than the things I hand back. He wants me to hand over myself.

reflections.title: The One Who Sits in the Heavens Laughs
reflections.html: Throughout the chapter the Philistine rulers make real decisions. They place the ark in Dagon’s temple, move it to Gath, move it to Ekron, and finally decide it must go back. Yet none of their decisions could overturn God’s purpose. Psalm 2 pictures the rulers of the earth taking counsel together against the LORD, and then says, “He who sits in the heavens shall laugh” (Psalm 2:4). God rules over history without turning human choices into illusions. He governs the outcome even when the people making the decisions do not worship Him.
reflections.q: Throughout the chapter the Philistine rulers make real decisions.

reflections.title: Running Out of Places to Put God
reflections.html: The Philistines treated the ark first as a trophy, then as a problem to relocate, and finally as something they had to send away. Each move seemed like a choice, but every choice narrowed the options until only one was left. Their freedom to move the ark had never been freedom from God’s authority. People can resist a truth that keeps growing clearer until every alternative has run out. But being forced by circumstances to let go is not the same as willingly submitting to God.
reflections.q: The Philistines treated the ark first as a trophy, then as a problem to relocate, and finally as something they had to send away.

reflections.title: We Never Had Control
reflections.html: The rulers decided where the ark went, again and again. Yet every decision showed the limits of their power, because God’s hand followed the ark wherever they sent it. We often spend great effort trying to keep control over things that depend on God anyway: our children’s choices, our health, the outcome of a decision at work. The fear of losing control keeps us from admitting that we never had the final say. Trust does not mean giving up responsibility. A parent still trains, a worker still plans, a leader still decides. But we do those things as stewards under God, not as the ones who finally determine how things turn out.
reflections.q: The rulers decided where the ark went, again and again.

12.brief: The men who do not die are stricken with tumors, and the cry of the city goes up to heaven. The chapter ends with the Philistines overwhelmed under the LORD’s hand.
12.explain:
“And the men who did not die were stricken with the tumors,”

Those who survived the plague still suffered. Death and disease spread throughout the city. No one in Ekron escaped the LORD's hand.

“and the cry of the city went up to heaven.”

The chapter ends with a cry rising from Ekron. “Went up to heaven” shows how great and desperate the outcry was. The language recalls Israel in Egypt, when “their cry came up to God because of the bondage” (Exodus 2:23). The irony is sharp: the Philistines, who had celebrated the capture of Israel's God, now raised a cry of anguish heavenward. Dagon could not help them. The chapter that began with the ark as a captive trophy ends with the captors overwhelmed and pleading to be rid of it. Chapter 6 will tell how they sent it home.
12.notes: Chapter 4 ends with a cry in Shiloh (4:13–14) and a mother's lament over departed glory; chapter 5 ends with a cry rising from Ekron.

hearing.observe: “The cry of the city went up to heaven,” yet the chapter does not record the Philistines praying to the God of Israel or turning to Him. The words recall Israel in Egypt, when “their cry came up to God because of the bondage” (Exodus 2:23). Two chapters later, Israel faces the Philistines again and begs Samuel, “Do not cease to cry out to the LORD our God for us,” and “the LORD answered him” (7:8–9). Scripture is full of cries of faith: blind Bartimaeus calling, “Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me!” (Mark 10:47), and Peter crying, “Lord, save me!” as he sank (Matthew 14:30). What matters is not how loud the cry is, but to whom it is addressed.
hearing.hear: Crying out in pain is not the same as turning to God. I can groan under pressure, complain and weep, and still not turn toward Him. God does not need polished words; He hears the groaning of those who come to Him. But I want my pain to bring me to Him, not just to rise somewhere in the air. And I can remember that Jesus “always lives to make intercession” for those who come to God through Him (Hebrews 7:25).

hearing.observe: Ekron wanted the ark sent away. Yet the cry of the city still went up to heaven. The people wanted distance from the God whose power they feared, and their anguish rose toward heaven anyway. The text does not say what each person meant by that cry or whether anyone addressed it to the LORD. It simply shows that the God they wanted to shut out remained the Lord over their circumstances, and their suffering was not hidden from heaven.
hearing.hear: People can push God away and still find themselves crying toward heaven when trouble comes. I have done it myself, keeping Him at a distance until I was desperate. Scripture tells me “the LORD is near to those who have a broken heart” (Psalm 34:18), and His invitation to come to Him still stands. I don’t want to wait for a crisis. I want to welcome Him near before the cry comes.

reflections.title: Surviving Is Not Being Brought to God
reflections.html: The text separates those who died from those who survived but were still struck with tumors (5:12). Avoiding the worst did not mean the problem was solved. The rulers had wanted the ark returned so their people would stop dying (5:11). The chapter records no request for forgiveness and no desire to know the LORD. They wanted deliverance from judgment without reconciliation with the Judge. Paul draws the same line: “godly sorrow produces repentance leading to salvation… but the sorrow of the world produces death” (2 Corinthians 7:10). People often see their need to escape suffering, guilt or fear long before they see their need for God Himself. Jesus does more than rescue His people from consequences. He “suffered once for sins, the just for the unjust, that He might bring us to God” (1 Peter 3:18). Getting through a crisis is a mercy, but the greater mercy is being brought to Him.
reflections.q: The text separates those who died from those who survived but were still struck with tumors (5:12).

reflections.title: Suffering Exposes What We Trusted
reflections.html: The final cry of Ekron came after the failure of everything the Philistines trusted: their army, their god and their rulers. None of them could save. Suffering can expose hidden dependencies and show where our hope has really been placed. That does not mean every hardship is a punishment. But one purpose of suffering is that it can expose the inadequacy of what we trusted in place of God, and turn us to honest reflection, humility and renewed trust in Him.
reflections.q: The final cry of Ekron came after the failure of everything the Philistines trusted: their army, their god and their rulers.
